## Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author)

### Review of the manuscript

“Climate outweighs human effects on vegetation assemblage dynamics in the Holocene” by Felde et al.

The manuscript submitted by Felde et al. presents a substantial contribution to the field of paleoecology. The study is based on a large dataset of pollen records spanning all continents to investigate the relative influence of climate and human activity on vegetation compositional changes throughout the Holocene. The authors use modelled climate data and archaeological radiocarbon dates, along with expert knowledge on human activities derived from pollen records, to disentangle the effects of climate and human activities on vegetation/pollen composition and diversity. The analytical framework is well developed, employing state-of-the-art statistical methods to explore large-scale pollen composition and diversity changes. The use of Pollen Assemblage Properties (PAPs) to assess compositional changes is innovative and adds a new dimension to paleoecological interpretation. Overall, this is an important and ambitious manuscript that I highly recommend for publication.

My major comments on the manuscript are listed below.

> **Response.** We thank the reviewer for the constructive assessment. The revision defines more carefully the ecological meaning of the pollen assemblage properties, the historical interval and spatial scales to which the conclusions apply, and the strengths and limitations of the climate and archaeological evidence.

### Scope and framing of the study period

The title suggests an analysis of the entire Holocene, yet the dataset ends approximately 2000 years ago. This period excludes the last two millennia, during which anthropogenic impacts on vegetation intensified, including major deforestation events and agricultural expansion. The title should be revised to more accurately reflect the temporal scope of the data and findings.
Furthermore, some statements in the discussion, such as the caution against the narrative that human transformation is always destructive, may appear strong given the temporal cut-off at 2 ka BP. I suggest to soften or contextualize this statement to avoid misinterpretation.

> **Response.** We agree. The title now specifies the interval 8.5–2.0 ka BP and refers to pollen assemblage dynamics. This is the period for which the archaeological SPD evidence supports the principal comparison. Some expert-identified events occur after 2.0 ka BP, but these younger observations are shown separately and do not extend the principal conclusion into the last two millennia. We have also removed the broad statement that human transformation was not destructive. The revised Discussion instead emphasises that our result concerns the spatially aggregated ecological patterns represented in this study and does not diminish the extensive historical and palaeoecological evidence for substantial local human transformation.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The title is now “Climate outweighs human effects on pollen assemblage dynamics from 8.5 to 2.0 ka BP.” The same temporal and ecological scope is maintained in the Abstract, hypotheses, Results, Discussion, and Conclusion. Younger event observations are identified separately in Fig. 4.

### Use and justification of climate model outputs and human activity proxies

While the use of paleoclimate model data is justified by the limited spatial coverage of proxy-based climate reconstructions, a brief discussion of the benefits and limitations of using model outputs (e.g., smoothed trends and difficulties to simulate climate in some regions) should be included. This will help the readers to better understand the implications using climate model outputs.

> **Response.** We agree and have added a fuller discussion. CHELSA-TraCE21k provides a spatially continuous and internally consistent description of climatic change across regions where proxy reconstructions remain uneven. This is valuable for a global comparison, but the simulations smooth short-lived and local climatic variation, depend on model assumptions, and may not reproduce conditions within the actual pollen source area, especially where elevation or topography changes over short distances. We therefore interpret the climate variables as broad representations of climatic history rather than exact reconstructions of the environments surrounding individual sites.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The advantages and limitations of the simulated climate histories are now explained under “Palaeoclimate” and revisited in the Discussion when comparing local ecological change with broad climatic patterns.

In a same way, the use of summed probability densities (SPDs) from archaeological radiocarbon dates is appropriate but should be more critically discussed, although the authors already mention some of the issues. These can underestimate human presence, especially in regions or periods with sparse data. Furthermore, the expert-derived “human-impact events” from pollen data introduce a degree of circular reasoning as it is based on pollen information. The authors should mention the pros and cons of using such approach.

> **Response.** We agree. We retain archaeological SPDs as validated proxies for regional human population changes, while making clear that they are histories of dated archaeological activity rather than direct censuses of past populations. Their form is influenced by preservation, calibration, archaeological research traditions, and uneven knowledge among regions and periods. SPD remains the principal human-history proxy because it is independent of the pollen response and can be compared across much of the study area. The expert-derived events contribute a different kind of evidence: regionally informed indications of land use and vegetation disturbance within pollen diagrams. They can reveal changes not represented by a regional SPD, but they are unevenly available and partly circular because both the event and the ecological response may be inferred from the same pollen sequence. We therefore use them to examine sensitivity to the choice of historical evidence, not as independent confirmation.

> **Changes in the revised article.** These complementary strengths and limitations are now explained in the Methods and Discussion. The Supplementary Information shows how the results change when archaeological SPDs, expert-derived events, or both are used to represent human activity.

### Background information and previous studies

The introduction would benefit from presenting a bit more prior studies that used similar approaches, e.g., Kuosmanen et al. (2018), Marquer et al. (2017), and Reitalu et al. (2015). These studies provide an important context for methods, data types, and interpretations of vegetation change drivers, although for Europe and regional scales only. Their inclusion would strengthen the rationale for the current study.

> **Response.** We agree that the regional literature is essential context. The Discussion now relates our study to European and other regional attempts to separate climatic and human influences on past vegetation. We also clarify an important ecological distinction: our response variables describe richness, evenness, turnover, and other properties of pollen assemblages, whereas several earlier studies reconstructed changes in particular taxa or vegetation composition.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The revised text discusses Kuosmanen et al. (2018), Marquer et al. (2017), Reitalu et al. (2013) on climatic and human influences on forest composition, and Reitalu et al. (2015) on functional and phylogenetic diversity inferred from pollen.

### Interpretation of hypotheses and results

Hypothesis 1 states that if human impact is an important driver, its influence should match or exceed that of climate. I would say “the major driver” rather than “important driver” in the case it exceeds climate.

> **Response.** We agree and now describe human activity as the proposed “primary driver” in H1. This wording reflects the intended comparison with climate without implying that a smaller estimated contribution would make human influence ecologically unimportant.

> **Changes in the revised article.** H1 now reads: “The first hypothesis (H1) proposed that human impact was the primary driver of changes in PAPs at continental-group and regional scales between 8.5 and 2.0 ka BP.”

The authors conclude that climate dominates vegetation change at large spatial scales rather than local scales. This aligns with prior studies. I agree with the authors and clearly support the fact that at finer spatial resolutions, human impacts become more visible and potentially dominant.
It is important to mention that the use of PAPs may homogenize vegetation signals and amplify climate-related patterns. This should be acknowledged.

> **Response.** We agree and now distinguish the geographical coherence of a driver from the ecological importance of its local effects. Climatic change can produce related responses across widely separated pollen sequences, whereas cultivation, burning, grazing, woodland clearance, and settlement often have intense but spatially heterogeneous effects. Summarising pollen assemblage properties across continental-group and regional units may therefore accentuate the coherent climatic component while obscuring diverse local histories of land use. The revised interpretation makes this scale dependence explicit.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The Discussion now cautions that the broad climatic pattern should not be used to discount well-supported local histories of human transformation. It also explains how the spatial extent of pollen recruitment, archaeological evidence, and analytical regions affects the comparison.

The manuscript would be greatly improved if the authors provide a discussion of vegetation changes themselves, and how specific taxa or assemblage types respond to climatic or anthropogenic drivers. Such discussion would help ecological interpretations.

> **Response.** We agree that the ecological interpretation required expansion. Richness records how many pollen types were detected; evenness describes how evenly they were represented; turnover and rate of change indicate the degree to which assemblages were reorganised through time. These properties can reflect migration, community reassembly, changes in dominance, disturbance, and land use. They are also shaped by pollen productivity and dispersal, basin setting, taxonomic resolution, and sampling effort. We therefore interpret them as properties of the pollen assemblage and avoid attributing a climatic or human contribution to particular trees, grasses, crops, or disturbance indicators without a taxon-level analysis.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The Discussion now explains the ecological meaning of each family of pollen assemblage properties and distinguishes this approach from reconstructions of particular taxa or land-cover classes.

### Data representativeness and site characteristics

The choice of 1262 pollen sequences is impressive, but more information is needed about the selection criteria. I would have assumed that much more sites would be available at such spatial scales.

> **Response.** We have expanded the account of how the pollen archive was assembled. Duplicate sequences were removed; samples outside the study interval or lacking adequate chronological control were excluded; each retained sample contained at least 25 terrestrial pollen grains; and each sequence contained at least five usable samples. Taxonomic names were harmonised before the assemblage properties were calculated. Africa was not included because the available sequences were too sparse when the compilation was assembled to support comparable regional analyses. This procedure yielded `r format(preparation_pool_n, big.mark = ",")` prepared sequences, of which `r format(original_h1_inventory_n, big.mark = ",")` entered the original H1 spatial analysis. Particular analyses use fewer sequences where the necessary climate, archaeological, ecological, or control information is absent.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The full selection criteria are now listed under “Data filtering.” Supplementary Table S1 and the guide at the beginning of this letter identify the sequences or regional comparisons represented in each analysis. Because the original search did not retain a complete count of every potentially available public sequence, we do not present the prepared collection as a fully quantified global census of pollen sequences.

Site characteristics (e.g., basin size, proximity to human settlements) can significantly influence pollen source area and the sensitivity to land use signals. This aspect, although mentioned by the authors, should be discussed a bit more in details, especially when interpreting local vs regional patterns.

> **Response.** We agree. Basin size and depositional setting determine how much of the surrounding vegetation contributes pollen to a sequence, while distance from settlements or cultivated land affects the likelihood that local land use will be recorded. These differences are ecologically important when a site-scale pollen signal is compared with an archaeological history assembled over hundreds of kilometres. Consistent information on basin geometry, depositional environment, and settlement proximity is unavailable for much of the global compilation, so these factors could not be represented uniformly in the models. We consequently restrict the interpretation to broad spatial patterns and discuss why individual sites may depart from them.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The Methods and Discussion now give greater attention to basin setting, pollen source area, and the contrast between local land-use histories and broad archaeological neighbourhoods. A separate comparison shows how the results change when dates are drawn from 250 rather than 500 km around a pollen site.

The analysis assumes stable spatial climate zones. However, climate zones have shifted over the Holocene, which could affect interpretations of vegetation-climate relationships. A brief discussion of this dynamic would be valuable.

> **Response.** We agree that climatic boundaries moved during the Holocene. We now call the five broad geographical units *continental groups* and their smaller analytical subdivisions *regions*. The regions were defined reproducibly from present-day Köppen–Geiger classes to divide the sequences into groups that are easier to compare. This is a practical classification, not a claim that these are natural, permanent, or uniquely correct ecological boundaries. A site assigned to a region using its modern Köppen–Geiger class may have experienced different climatic conditions in the past. The continuous palaeoclimate histories, rather than the fixed regional assignments, provide the climatic evidence in the fitted models.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The Methods now define *continental groups* and *regions* and explain why the regions were formed. Figure captions, tables, and the Discussion use these terms consistently and state the limits of a fixed modern classification.

### Thresholds for pollen counts

The decision to lower the minimum pollen count threshold from 150 to 25 grains per sample raises some questions about data quality. A threshold as low as 25 may introduce significant noise and reduce the reliability of PAPs. The rationale for this decision should be clearly explained and its implications discussed.

> **Response.** We agree that small pollen counts make richness, evenness, and turnover less precise. We have clarified that 25 grains is the minimum for retaining an individual sample, whereas 150 grains is the usual rarefaction target. A lower sequence-specific target is used only when a sequence cannot consistently support 150 grains. Retaining these sequences preserves evidence from regions where pollen archives are sparse. We also quantified the geographical cost of more demanding targets. A target of 300 grains retains `r pollen_retention[["n_records_retained"]][pollen_retention[["threshold"]] == 300]` of `r preparation_pool_n` sequences; a target of 500 grains retains `r pollen_retention[["n_records_retained"]][pollen_retention[["threshold"]] == 500]`; and a target of 1,000 grains retains only `r pollen_retention[["n_records_retained"]][pollen_retention[["threshold"]] == 1000]`. The losses are strongly uneven among regions and periods, so stricter filtering would narrow both the quantity and historical representativeness of the evidence. These comparisons raise the rarefaction target and its associated minimum; they do not require every sample to contain 300 or 500 grains, and they do not constitute a refitted H1 analysis at those strict minima.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The Methods now distinguish the 25-grain sample minimum, the requirement that more than half of samples in a retained count-based sequence meet the 150-grain target, and the lower rarefaction targets used for some retained sequences. Supplementary Fig. S23 and Supplementary Table S3 show how stricter targets reduce regional and temporal coverage, and the Discussion treats finite counts and pollen production as limitations on ecological interpretation.

### Figures

Figure 4 shows a lot of information, and the plots are
too small. It is difficult to see the major patterns. Furthermore, the panel labels in Figure 2 appear to be misaligned (E and D).

> **Response.** We agree and have reorganised the figures around the ecological sequence of the argument. Fig. 1 introduces the study design. Fig. 2 then shows six representative histories of pollen assemblage change, with all ten properties presented in Supplementary Figs. S12–S21. Figs. 3 and 4 compare the climatic and human contributions in space and through time. The former H2 figure is now Supplementary Fig. S10, and the remaining robustness analyses are grouped in the Supplementary Information.

> **Changes in the revised article.** Figs. 2–4 now each address one principal question at a readable scale, and their captions identify the evidence, temporal or spatial controls, and treatment of uncertain estimates.

This manuscript provides a novel and valuable analysis of Holocene vegetation dynamics at broad spatial scales. The conclusions are well supported, and my major comments focus on some aspects of the methods and interpretation that require clarification and additional nuance. By addressing these issues, the manuscript will be greatly improved. Again, I recommend publication after these revisions are done.

> **Response.** We thank the reviewer again. The revised article now places the statistical comparison within a clearer account of the pollen archive, the historical proxies, the spatial scale of ecological change, and the limits of broad-scale inference.
